feedback: When an observation doesn't fit, highlight the strain on the old model (e.g. the extra circle bolted on for Mars' retrograde loop) so the learner feels the model being pushed, not just told it is wrong.

After revising, show the heliocentric model re-explaining the observations gathered in this activity, reinforcing that a revised idea must account for the old evidence as well as the new — while itself staying open to revision.
Frame the moment of revision with a 'strength' cue — science self-corrected — rather than an 'error' or 'failure' cue.

On the final sort, if a learner labels a best-supported explanation as 'just an opinion', prompt them to point to the evidence behind it; if they treat an opinion as settled science, ask what evidence would test it.
activities.intendedInsight: Revision is an evidence-driven mechanism: the old idea was the best explanation for the evidence people HAD, and when better evidence arrived science did not collapse — it upgraded and became stronger. The new model earns its place by accounting for the observations the old one could AND the ones it could not, while itself remaining a best-current explanation open to revision.
learnerActions: Start with the accepted model: Earth sits still at the centre and everything circles it — note that at first it seems to work, so you accept it.

Feed observations into the model one at a time from an evidence tray and judge for each whether the current model fits it or not: 'Mars sometimes loops backwards across the sky' (the geocentric model needs an awkward extra circle to cope), 'Through a telescope, Venus shows phases like the Moon' (a model with Venus circling Earth cannot fit the full set of phases), 'Through his telescope, Galileo saw four moons orbiting Jupiter, not Earth' (another mismatch with 'everything circles Earth').
Watch mismatches accumulate until a REVISE option becomes available; choose to revise, swapping in the Sun-centred model.
Re-test the revised Sun-centred model against each of these earlier observations and confirm that it now accounts for all three.
Note that the Sun-centred model is itself a new best-current explanation — stronger because it fits more evidence, but still open to further revision, not a final perfect answer.
At the end, sort statements into 'this is our best-supported explanation, open to revision' versus 'that's just an opinion', so provisional is never mistaken for 'anything goes'.
activities.title: The 'Best Idea So Far' machine: overturn a model with evidence

feedback: Keep the figure welcoming of challenge and anchored to specific observations, redirecting if the conversation drifts into opinion or bare storytelling.
When the learner asks a sharp evidence question, have the figure reward it by explaining exactly which observation forced the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Changing your mind in the light of evidence is honest and is what science is for; this builds the affective sense that openness to revision is a strength, told from inside a real human change of view.
learnerActions: Take the role of an interviewer and question a historical or expert figure at the moment an accepted worldview is crumbling (e.g. an astronomer as the geocentric picture breaks down).
Challenge the figure: ask why they are changing a belief they once held, and what specific evidence turned them.
Press for evidence, not just anecdote — ask 'what did you observe?' and 'why didn't the old idea fit?'
Ask whether being shown to be mistaken means they failed, and listen to them explain why revising an idea in light of evidence is the point of science, not a defeat.
activities.title: Interview a scientist who lived a revision

feedback: Connect the apparent loop back to the relative motion of Earth and Mars (Earth overtaking Mars) rather than to a single central, still Earth.
Keep the scope to the astronomy example and relate it back to the general lesson that a wider body of evidence, not retrograde motion alone, supported the change.
activities.intendedInsight: Different models can account for the same observation in different ways. Here the Sun-centred arrangement explains Mars’s apparent backward loop through relative motion, while Earth-centred models used epicycles; judging the models involves a wider body of evidence.
learnerActions: Examine how Mars appears to loop backwards when viewed from Earth. Compare how an Earth-centred model uses epicycles to represent this observation with how a Sun-centred model explains it through the relative motions of Earth and Mars.
Compare how the Sun-centred arrangement, with Earth also moving, explains the apparent loop as a viewing effect of two moving bodies.

Explain how both models account for the apparent loop, and describe how Earth overtaking Mars provides the Sun-centred account. Consider this alongside the other observations in the activity rather than treating retrograde alone as decisive proof.
activities.title: Astronomy close-up: how the old and new models explained retrograde motion differently

feedback: Full response: explains past scientists reasoned soundly from their evidence, that revision on new evidence is a strength, and that current ideas are provisional-but-best — and transfers this to a fresh example.

Partial response (e.g. only 'we got better telescopes'): acknowledge that new instruments did matter in this case, then discuss how the SAME evidence can sometimes support a new explanation without new tools (a reinterpretation, not just a new machine), and ask why revision is a strength rather than just a fact.

Gap response ('old scientists were stupid', or 'science is proven and won't change', or 'they keep changing it so you can't trust it'): reteach with a case where a 'certain' idea changed (continents don't move -> plate tectonics), and walk through why the geocentric view was reasonable given that the Sun really does appear to cross the sky.
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrate that you can hold BOTH that the old view was reasonable for its evidence AND that current views remain open to revision, while keeping provisional distinct from mere opinion.
learnerActions: Answer 'why did scientists change this idea?' for a revision you have met, naming the specific evidence that forced the change.
Match old ideas to the evidence that revised them.
Sort statements into 'best current explanation (evidence-based, open to revision)' versus 'just an opinion / anything goes'.

Respond in writing to the prompt: 'Long ago most people, including most scientists, were sure the Sun moved around the Earth; now we say the Earth moves around the Sun. Does that mean the old scientists were foolish? And might what scientists tell us today change too? Explain your thinking.'
activities.title: Explain and sort: check the understanding
